accueil.activitesIntro: The common thread in everything I do: meeting people, observing them, and drawing as a way to create an experience or tell a story.

activites.description: I draw guests, artists and key moments of an event live on site, to create unique memories.
I hand-draw original portraits on paper from your photos, to give as a gift or keep as a one-of-a-kind memory.
I draw performers live, on stage or backstage, to capture the energy of a show and the people behind it.
I film my encounters and drawings to tell human stories on Instagram and TikTok, blending drawing, conversation and humor.
I turn my observations and thoughts on human relationships and society into simple, accessible, spontaneous drawings and comics.

accueil.bio: Anne Leblanc is a French illustrator, content creator and author. Fascinated by people — their faces, their habits, their small contradictions — she observes before drawing, and draws to better understand. Live portraits, live drawing, comics or collaborations: through very simple forms, she turns what she observes into accessible human stories that make people want to look at the world differently.

questions.q: What does Anne offer at an event?
questions.r: Anne draws the people present and the moments unfolding in front of her, right there on site. She can create individual, couple, or group portraits, as well as capture spontaneous moments and interactions between guests. The goal isn't just to leave with a drawing: the drawing also creates a real experience and a moment of connection with the people she meets.

questions.q: What types of events can Anne work at?
questions.r: Anne can work at both private and professional events: weddings, birthdays, private parties, brand events, product launches, corporate events, festivals, trade shows, conferences, performances or cultural events. She can also design more specific formats with a brand, an artist or an agency. If a project doesn't exactly match these examples, it's still worth getting in touch to discuss it.

questions.q: How does a live drawing service work?
questions.r: Anne arrives at the venue with her materials and sets up somewhere she can move around easily and see the guests. She can then go meet the people she draws, or be set up at a designated spot where guests come to her. She draws right there on site and favors a spontaneous approach: people don't necessarily need to sit for a long pose. The exact format is worked out beforehand based on the type of event, the number of guests, and the time available.

questions.q: Do guests need to pose?
questions.r: No. Anne can draw portraits from a short pose, but she also likes to observe people in their environment and capture spontaneous attitudes or moments. For some events, she may create surprise portraits, choosing herself the people or moments she finds interesting to draw.

questions.q: How many people can Anne draw during an event?
questions.r: It depends on the format, the number of hours she's present, and the type of drawings wanted. An individual portrait usually takes around fifteen minutes when done at an event, though the pace can vary depending on the level of detail and the chosen format. Rather than promising a fixed number of portraits, Anne prefers to set a realistic goal based on the event. If a large number of people need to be drawn, it's best to mention this in the request so she can suggest the most suitable format.

questions.q: Are the drawings finished and handed over on the same day?
questions.r: When the format of the service allows it, drawings are made and handed directly to guests during the event. For certain projects requiring more time or a particular level of finish, drawings may be completed or sent afterward. The details are specified in the quote.

questions.q: Can Anne draw things other than portraits?
questions.r: Yes. She can draw scenes, couples, groups, interactions between several people, or particular moments of the event. The drawing can also be adapted to a specific concept designed together with the client.

questions.q: Can a service be customized for a brand or an event?
questions.r: Yes. The service can be designed around the identity of a brand, an event, or a campaign: the drawing format, paper, presentation, incorporating a product or a visual world, staging the service, etc. Anne can also work with an agency or a brand to develop a more original concept around drawing.

questions.q: Can Anne work at a wedding?
questions.r: Yes. Live drawing can take place during the cocktail hour, the reception drinks, or part of the celebration. Anne can draw the couple, guests, groups, or particular spontaneous moments of the day. Since every wedding is different, the format is worked out with the couple or the organizer based on the day's schedule and the number of guests.

questions.q: Does Anne travel?
questions.r: Yes. Anne is based in Paris and can travel within France and abroad for projects. Any travel, transport, and accommodation costs are added on top when the project requires it. These are clearly stated in the quote.

questions.q: How far in advance should I book?
questions.r: The earlier the better, especially for weddings, major events, and projects requiring travel. That said, it's still possible to contact Anne for an event coming up soon — she'll simply let you know if she's available. The date is only confirmed once the quote is accepted, under the terms stated in it.

questions.q: Does Anne take custom orders?
questions.r: Yes. Anne hand-draws custom portraits from photographs. She mainly works on Bristol paper with alcohol markers and colored pencils. Prices depend on the size and the number of people depicted (see the pricing table above).

questions.q: Can I order a drawing with several people?
questions.r: Yes. Anne can create portraits of couples, families, groups of friends, or several people brought together in a single drawing. The price varies according to the size and the number of people.

questions.q: Can I request personalized elements in the drawing?
questions.r: Yes. Certain particular elements can be added: objects, animals, clothing, settings, places, accessories, or other details that matter to the client. Requests requiring extra work may incur a surcharge, which will be indicated before the order is confirmed.

questions.q: Can I request a rush order?
questions.r: Yes, depending on Anne's availability. The usual turnaround is currently about 2 weeks, not including any shipping time. A rush request may incur a surcharge depending on the timeframe requested and her workload. Anne always confirms whether it's possible and the price before starting.

questions.q: What kind of photos does Anne work from?
questions.r: Anne works from photographs provided by the client. Faces should ideally be clearly visible, sharp, and well lit so she can observe them properly. If unsure between several photos, the client can send them all with the request so Anne can suggest the one that seems best suited.

questions.q: How long does it take to receive an order?
questions.r: The usual turnaround is currently about 2 weeks, plus any shipping time. The exact timeframe is confirmed when the order is placed. For a rush order, it's best to contact Anne before confirming so she can check her availability.

questions.q: Does Anne only take on live drawing services?
questions.r: No. She's also open to projects that use drawing in other ways: content creation, collaborations with artists or creators, custom comics, illustration, artistic performances, editorial projects, brand concepts, or hybrid formats between drawing and video. If a project doesn't fit a specific category, it's still worth pitching the idea to her.

questions.q: Can Anne create content for a brand?
questions.r: Yes. Anne can design content around her world: drawing, encounters, portraits, conversation, humor, or discovering a person, a place, or a product. She can also take part in shaping the format when a project calls for creative input. Publishing, production, and usage terms for the content are defined case by case.

questions.q: Can Anne draw a public figure or an artist?
questions.r: Yes. Anne especially enjoys projects that combine drawing, encounters, and performance. For example, she can create an artist's portrait, draw someone during an interview or meeting, take part around a show, or design content around a public figure.

questions.q: Can Anne perform on stage?
questions.r: Yes. She can take part in a show or cultural event and draw a performer, a speaker, or a scene live. The format depends on the project: drawing during a performance, a live drawing show, creating a live portrait, video content around the appearance, etc.

questions.q: Can Anne's services lead to content on her social media?
questions.r: Not necessarily. When it's relevant and with the agreement of those involved, Anne may film certain moments of her services and turn them into content for her social media. This can be planned from the start with the client if they'd also like content around the event. Creating and publishing that content may then be handled as a separate service.

questions.q: Can I ask Anne to create a video in addition to the drawing?
questions.r: Yes. Anne can design formats that combine drawing and video: meeting someone, an interview while drawing, behind-the-scenes footage from an event, reactions to the portrait, etc. The content can be intended for her social media, the client's, or both, depending on the project. Usage rights and distribution terms are defined in advance.

questions.q: Where can I find Anne's prices?
questions.r: Prices for custom portrait orders are listed on the dedicated “Portrait Commission” page, so clients can get a first idea of the budget before contacting Anne. For events, collaborations, artistic services, and professional projects, Anne mainly works on a quote basis, since the price depends on the shape of the project.

questions.q: Why are event services quote-based?
questions.r: A service can vary enormously depending on: how long Anne is present, the type of event, the number of guests, the number and type of drawings wanted, the location, travel, the level of customization, any content creation involved, and the client's specific needs. Anne therefore prefers to put together a tailored quote rather than list a single price that wouldn't fit every project.

questions.q: How do I request a quote?
questions.r: The contact form above lets you share the key details of your project. The more specific the request, the more effectively Anne can respond.

questions.q: How quickly does Anne respond?
questions.r: Anne does her best to respond to professional inquiries and orders as quickly as possible. Response time can vary depending on her workload and travel schedule. If a project has an important or upcoming date, it's best to mention it clearly in the message.

questions.q: What happens after I submit a request?
questions.r: Once Anne receives the request, she checks the project's feasibility and her availability. If the project is a good fit, she'll discuss the client's needs if needed and then send a quote. The service is confirmed once the quote is accepted, under the terms it states. For more complex projects, a detailed brief can also be worked out beforehand.

autre.titre: An idea that doesn't fit any category?
autre.texte: Tell her about it. Anne is especially interested in projects that use drawing in an original way: an event, a show, a brand, video, comics, an encounter, a performance, or an artistic project. There's no need to have already figured out the perfect format. An idea or a simple urge is enough to get in touch and think together about how to turn it into a project.

apropos.intro: Anne Leblanc is an illustrator based in Paris. Before she learned to draw, she first learned to look.

recit.texte: She started out at a theater school, which she attended for about 2 years — a first way of observing people: bodies, expressions, the way a presence can say something without speaking.
That time remains essential to my path — my work today is still deeply tied to observing others.

She then moved on to studying architecture and set design for two years — a shift driven by a desire to work with space, images and staging, and by a question at the heart of set design: how do you tell a story visually?

Her path then continued at the Théâtre de l'Européen: she has run it since the age of 23, balancing technical work and artistic direction. It's in this setting that she draws performers live on stage, including comedian Léopold Lemarchand, in front of about 350 people.
Drawing gradually became her main means of expression. In September 2024, she started posting her drawings on Instagram — first her friends, then strangers she met in the parks and streets of Paris.

What interests me is meeting someone, observing them for several minutes, and trying to understand what makes up their face, their attitude, their presence. I'm not trying to reproduce someone: for me, drawing is a way of truly looking at a person.

She loves drawing on the spot, wherever she is — at the beach, in a restaurant, in the street, in the middle of an event — as soon as she can pull out a notebook and a pen, with that immediate, unpredictable quality: observing someone, making choices very fast, and conveying something of them with very little. Filming her drawings and sharing them online became an important step in her path — both an artistic practice and a way of meeting people.

blocks.texte: Anne is naturally very observant: she likes watching people, listening to their conversations, noticing small details, understanding the dynamics between them — and can spend a lot of time trying to understand something before producing a response.

In her work, she tries to turn that observation into something creative: understanding, then simplifying it into an image — starting from something complex, a person, an emotion, an idea, and drawing out its essence. That's also what draws her to comics and to making things easy to understand: turning a complicated idea into something accessible through simple images.

Paper plays an important role in her practice. Anne has no interest in digitally reproducing the look of traditional drawing: she likes working with the material itself — paper, marker, pencil — and the happy accidents that can happen while drawing.

I wondered a lot whether I should switch to drawing on a tablet, like a lot of other illustrators do. But I realized I deeply love paper — today I want to make it a real strength, rather than something less modern.

She works on Bristol paper with alcohol markers and colored pencils for her portraits, and a lot with a ballpoint pen in a notebook. She likes the object to physically exist before it's digitized — scanning is simply a way of carrying a physical object into the digital world.

The encounter is at the heart of her practice. When Anne draws someone, it's never just about making their portrait — it's about talking with that person, discovering who they are, what they think, what they dream about. The drawing becomes an excuse for the encounter — and a small event in itself: you sit down, let yourself be observed for a few minutes, see your portrait, and walk away with something unexpected.

Anne is also drawn to systems and formats: taking in a lot of information, looking for the connections between it, then “wringing it out” until a central idea emerges. Today she wants to develop a practice that sits between drawing, observation, encounter, and sharing.

sections.titre: What she looks for in drawing

blocks.texte: Anne isn't after the most virtuosic or detailed drawing possible, but the right way to convey an idea to someone. Liv Strömquist's work reinforced that belief for her: the way she takes complex subjects — sociology, love, human relationships — and turns them into accessible comics shows that simplicity can be a strength.

She's also drawn to artists who turn something personal into something universal — an experience, a specific detail, that many people can recognize themselves in. It's a direction she'd like to keep developing in her own work.
